An introduction to CISA’s BOD 22-01

Issued nearly four years ago, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Binding Operational Directive 22-01 (BOD 22-01) has been adopted across both public and private sector organizations as a framework to ensure timely remediation of vulnerabilities being exploited by adversaries. By establishing a catalog of known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) and emphasizing a risk-based, prioritized approach, it provides a clear model for organizations to strengthen their cybersecurity posture and reduce exposure to real-world threats.

InsightGovCloud, Rapid7’s FedRAMP-authorized suite of security solutions, helps organizations implement BOD 22-01 by providing automated vulnerability scanning, real-time alerts for KEVs, and reporting aligned with regulatory requirements. Public and private sector teams can quickly identify at-risk assets, prioritize remediation efforts based on active exploitation, and maintain an auditable record of compliance. By leveraging our secure, cloud-based platform, organizations gain continuous visibility, streamlined vulnerability management, and the confidence that remediation aligns with federal cybersecurity standards.

How InsightGovCloud stacks up against key BOD 22-01 requirements

Requirement 1: Maintain continuous inventory and visibility

InsightVM, included in the suite, supports continuous and automated discovery of both external and internal assets through Discovery Connections, which allow organizations to continuously poll network sources like Active Directory, AWS, and Azure to enumerate connected hosts and launch scans.

For cloud environments, Rapid7 InsightCloudSec will continuously inventory the entire environment for the creation of new resources and automatically scan and assess those resources against compliance frameworks.

Rapid7 also maintains up-to-date inventory of CISA KEVs with an industry leading 90% coverage for both on-premise and cloud based host vulnerabilities.

Requirement 2: Remediate CISA KEV findings on a prioritized schedule

Continuous ingestion of CISA KEV catalog by Rapid7 ensures that detection and prioritization of KEV’s can be streamlined and native to one platform.

Automatically detect and triage assets with KEVs across cloud and hybrid environments.

Prioritize CISA KEV’s across your entire environment and establish remediation projects to quickly and collaboratively remediate KEVs.

Requirement 3: Establish policies and enforcement

Collaborative remediation and compliance goals automatically track and assign vulnerabilities to the right teams with organizational defined timelines and real time dashboards to measure progress.

Requirement 4: Automate reporting

Rapid7 has predefined exports in Cyberscope XML reporting format for seamless ingestion into reports for CyberScope submissions as per CyberScope Automated Data Feeds Submission Manual published by the U.S. Office of Management and Budget.

Built-in audit trail to demonstrate adherence with BOD 22-01.

Why agencies and contractors choose InsightGovCloud

Rapid7 InsightGovCloud is designed to support the rigorous requirements of state and local government agencies. The benefits are many, but among the top are its deployment into a FedRAMP Authorized environment – meeting federal security and compliance requirements at every level – its seamless integration into an existing security ecosystem, and its out-of-the-box alignment with CISA and CMMC security mandates.

Agencies and contractors enjoy a future-proof tool in that Rapid7 is continuously updating against the ever-growing KEV catalog, as well as unmatched visibility and control through leadership-friendly reporting. Get to know the platform better here.

Title: Simplify User Access Management with SCIM on Rapid7 Command Platform
Context: Keep user information current: Synchronize supported user attributes as information changes
Full Text:
Managing access to security tools shouldn't require another manual process. As organizations grow, keeping user accounts and permissions up to date becomes increasingly complex. Employees join, change roles, and leave, creating a constant need to update access across applications.

When these processes rely on manual administration, delays and oversights can introduce unnecessary work and security risk.

Rapid7 Command Platform now supports System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM), enabling customers to automate user provisioning and deprovisioning through their existing identity provider (IdP).

This helps organizations reduce administrative overhead, maintain more consistent access controls, and manage identity at scale.

Automate user access throughout the employee lifecycle

SCIM is an open standard that enables identity providers, such as Okta, to automatically manage user accounts in connected applications.

With SCIM enabled, Rapid7 Command Platform customers can:

Automate provisioning: Create accounts when employees join or need access.

Keep user information current: Synchronize supported user attributes as information changes.

Simplify offboarding: Automatically deactivate accounts when users no longer require access.

Manage groups at scale: Synchronize group membership to help streamline access administration.

Rather than manually updating accounts in Command Platform, administrators can manage supported identity lifecycle changes through their existing IdP.

Less administration, more consistent access control

Consider a common scenario: An employee leaves the organization. Without automated provisioning, an administrator must remember to deactivate that employee's access across their applications. If an account is missed, it could remain active longer than intended.

With SCIM, changes made in the organization's identity provider can automatically trigger corresponding account updates in Command Platform.

By introducing SCIM at the platform level, Rapid7 helps organizations:

Reduce operational overhead by eliminating repetitive account-management tasks.

Strengthen access governance by reducing stale accounts and keeping user information aligned with identity provider policies.

Scale more efficiently by centralizing identity lifecycle management for supported Command Platform applications.

For organizations with security and compliance requirements, these capabilities also help support consistent onboarding and offboarding processes.

Get started with SCIM

SCIM support is now available to Rapid7 Command Platform customers.

Platform administrators can configure SCIM through Command Platform's SSO settings using their existing identity provider. SCIM is disabled by default and requires configuration before automated provisioning begins.

For prerequisites and setup instructions, visit the Command Platform SCIM integration documentation.

This release adds multiple new modules, and 6 of those modules point at a single target: Langflow, the open-source LLM workflow builder. Together they cover an authentication bypass (CVE-2026-93680), 3 unauthenticated remote code execution paths (CVE-2026-0768, CVE-2026-0769, and CVE-2026-10134), and 2 authenticated code execution flaws (CVE-2026-7873 and CVE-2026-93674), spanning Langflow releases from 1.0.0 through 1.11.4. Thanks to the work of rmhowe425, with research credit to Peter Girnus and n0k0. Beyond Langflow, open source contributor kmkz contributed a pre-auth RCE chain against OpenCTI. MongoDB coverage has also been expanded with 3 new auxiliary modules plus an Apache Solr version scanner thanks to the work of community member h00die.

Title: Rapid7 Intelligence Wins the 2026 Péter Szőr Award for Outstanding Research
Context: This was back when malware analysis meant staring at assembly, arguing about what a routine really did, and realizing hours later that your first theory was wrong
Full Text:
Some awards you're happy to receive, while others make you stop for a moment. Receiving the 2026 Péter Szőr Award this week at Virus Bulletin in Seville for our research, BPFdoor in Telecom Networks: Sleeper Cells in the Backbone, was of the latter kind.

Virus Bulletin created the award to honor Péter's life and work, and it recognizes outstanding technical security research: the rigorous, the deep, and the useful – exactly what he was known for himself. And as far as recognitions in our industry go, it's hard to top. I'm extremely proud.

What the Pèter Szőr Award means to us

I knew Péter, and early in my career, I learned from him. This was back when malware analysis meant staring at assembly, arguing about what a routine really did, and realizing hours later that your first theory was wrong. One memory came straight back when I heard about the award: going through Stuxnet together. For anyone in research at the time, that was the moment you knew the game had changed. Engineering, tradecraft, espionage and physical-world consequences, all in one package.

What stayed with me wasn't how much Péter knew, but rather his curiosity. He wanted to understand things, and then once he did, he wanted everyone else to understand too. Plenty of brilliant people in cybersecurity keep it to themselves, but the ones who leave a legacy make the people around them better.

Receiving an award that carries his name felt like one of those full-circle moments.

The research behind the award

The original research from Rapid7 Intelligence emerged after months of investigating stealthy access inside telecommunications environments. This wasn't malware dropped during a conventional intrusion, but long-term strategic positioning: passive backdoors, kernel-level capabilities and covert access, quietly settled into critical infrastructure and in no hurry whatsoever.

Telecom networks carry our communications, our identities and, increasingly, everything governments and businesses run on. So when an adversary sets up camp there, the impact goes well beyond one compromised machine or one unlucky company.

Virus Bulletin's community nomination noted that the work paired deep technical investigation with real-world impact, including long hours with agencies and CERTs around the world and tools, scripts, intelligence and detection capabilities for defenders. That's the part I'm happiest about, as this wasn't research for publication alone. Remember that a PDF has never stopped an intrusion.

Publishing research is a checkpoint, not the finish line

We're still doing the research. Since the original report, Rapid7 Intelligence has analyzed hundreds more samples, found previously undocumented BPFDoor variants, and tracked changes in the operators' tradecraft. Our follow-up work covered new httpShell and icmpShell variants built to make detection even harder. In further publications, we went beyond BPFDoor to additional Linux implants and infrastructure targeting telecom and network-edge environments, including AVERAT and techniques that hide in ordinary-looking traffic like SMTP.

That's how this work goes. You find something, you share it, someone sends you another sample, a CERT spots something in their environment, an analyst notices the one odd function nobody looked at twice, and you're back down the rabbit hole. Anyone who thinks an initial report is the finish line has never received "just one more sample" at 4 p.m. on a Friday.

And truthfully, I also love that this happens in the open. From the outside, our industry looks like a cage match over attribution, naming conventions and whose acronym is cooler. But when something truly matters, researchers, vendors, CERTs and governments put that aside and share, because protecting people beats winning the naming argument.

This award belongs to the team: Rapid7 Intelligence

Research like this never belongs to just one or two people. It belongs to the analysts still staring at code after everyone else has gone home, the people who question an assumption because something doesn't add up, the people that keep the show running, and the detection engineers who turn findings into something defenders can use. It also belongs to the people collecting samples, maintaining infrastructure and correlating intelligence, and to the CERTs, agencies and peers who trusted us enough to share what they saw.

I'm proud of the Rapid7 Intelligence team, and not because of the trophy. I'm proud of why we got it: we took a hard problem, did the hard work, and then tried to make the result useful to someone else.

To the next generation of research

Today, the conversation has evolved to include autonomous agents, AI-generated malware and machine-speed attacks. Tomorrow it'll be something new. My motivation stays the same: I want to leave the digital world a little safer for the generations that come after us.

Somewhere right now, a young researcher is opening a debugger for the first time and wondering how on earth the thing works. Someone will investigate the Stuxnet of their generation, and someone will eventually sit in the chair I'm in now. Our job isn't just to detect today's attacks. It's to share what we learn, build tools, mentor people and make sure they start a few steps ahead of where we did.

Péter did that for our industry, and he did it for me.

Thank you to Virus Bulletin and our peers in the security community for this recognition, to everyone who contributed to the research, publicly or behind the scenes, and to Péter, who taught a young malware researcher that taking things apart is only half the job. The other half is making sure somebody else can learn from what you found.
